scribe_response.text: Is there a celebration you remember especially well? The celebration I remember best is my daughter Liza's wedding, Liza's wedding, three years ago in Abu Dhabi. It took a whole year to plan, and I was more nervous than the bride. Liza married a gentle doctor named Daniel, um whose family came from Kerala. So we had two cultures and two kitchens at one table. We held the ceremony in our church on a Friday evening in November. I spent months sewing sixteen little gowns um in yellow silk for the flower girls. My fingers were sore, and I found pins in my cushions, my slippers, and once my sandwich. Ramon was in charge of the food, and he cooked for four days with his uh brother. They made a mountain of pancit for long life, because, because noodles must never be cut short. There was also lechon, a whole roasted pig, which arrived in a van with its own driver. Daniel's mother brought a huge pot of biryani, and the kitchens argued happily for hours. On the wedding morning I woke before dawn and sat on the balcony with strong tea. The sky was soft peach, the city was silent, and um time seemed to hold its breath. What happened next? When I helped Liza into her gown, my hands trembled so much I could barely fasten the buttons. She looked at me in the mirror, and I saw the little girl under um my sewing table. Her veil was made from my own mother's lace, which I had carried across the sea. My choir sang during the ceremony, and I stood among uh the sopranos with tears on my face. I could hardly manage the high notes, but the others carried me along. Ramon walked Liza down the aisle in a gray suit, uh and his chin shook. He whispered something to her, um and later she told me it was a promise. After the vows we stepped outside under a shower of rice and paper flowers. The children ran in circles, and one little boy fell asleep under a table. The uh reception was in a garden strung with golden lights and scented with jasmine. My friends from the choir sang a surprise song, an old Filipino love song. Then came the karaoke, which I had uh been waiting for all evening. I took the microphone and sang a song Ramon had loved since our courting days. He sat at the front table, watching me with his old, shy, sailor's smile. Can you tell me more about that? Even Daniel's grandfather, a serious man who rarely spoke, stood up and clapped um in rhythm. We danced until the um musicians were exhausted, and the cake looked like a battlefield. Paolo made a speech and teased his sister so much that she threw a bread roll at him. Everyone howled, and the photographer caught it, and that picture hangs in my hallway. At the end of the uh party Liza kissed my forehead and thanked me for everything. I could not speak, so I held her face the uh way my mother held mine. The guests drifted away, and the staff began folding chairs and sweeping confetti. Ramon and I sat on the steps with our shoes off and our feet aching beautifully. He said the pig had been a triumph, and I said the bride had been one. We agreed that um both statements were true. I have been to many celebrations, in villages and cities and even on ships. But that night, with um two families and two kitchens, felt like the whole world sitting down together. Memory keeps the smells longer than it keeps the faces. I hope that when I am, I am very old, I still remember jasmine and roasted pig.
